title: New wine (Mark 2:18–22)
hook: you don't pour new wine into old skins

segments.voice: Yesterday: Levi's table, a tax collector's dinner, and Jesus sitting with the people nobody sat with. Your line was the doctor is for the sick.

Someone at work notices you're not doing it the way it's always been done. Not wrong, just different. And they ask, a little sharply, why? That's where today's story starts. The followers of John the Baptist fast. The Pharisees fast. Serious religious people go without food on set days, and everyone knows it. But Jesus's followers are eating. So people ask him straight out: why don't your disciples fast? He answers with a wedding, a patched coat, and a wineskin about to burst.

First the wedding. In the King James Bible: "Can the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them?" The children of the bridechamber are the wedding guests. Nobody fasts at a wedding. You eat, you dance, the party goes for days. While the groom is here, Jesus says, it's a feast. But he adds a shadow: the day will come when the groom is taken away, and then they'll fast. Christians hear that as his first hint at his death, and it's why most churches still keep fasts, in Lent and on other days. Then the coat. You don't sew a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old coat; the first wash, it shrinks and tears a worse hole. Then the wine. "No man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles." A bottle here is a skin, usually goat, not glass. New wine is still fermenting, still giving off gas, so it needs a fresh skin that can stretch. An old skin is dry and stiff; it splits, and you lose both. So what's the new wine? Christians usually say it's what Jesus himself brings, and that it needs room to move. How that applies is argued in every generation, from reformers to people who start a new kind of church in a coffee shop. And Luke, telling the same story, adds a line that keeps everyone humble: people who have drunk the old wine say the old is better. New wine isn't a verdict on the old. It's a question of what can hold it.
screen: `NOBODY FASTS AT A WEDDING.` · `A NEW PATCH TEARS AN OLD COAT.` · `A SKIN FOR WINE THAT'S STILL ALIVE.` · `THE OLD IS BETTER, SOME SAY.`

segments.voice: Choose something you do the same way every day: how you pray, if you pray, how you greet the people you live with, how you start work, the walk you always take. Notice whether it still holds what it's meant to hold, or whether it's gone a bit stiff. Don't throw it out; just pick one small change, a different time, a different word, a different route, and hold it lightly.
New wine. Wine still fermenting, too alive for an old stiff skin. It needs a vessel that can stretch.
Your line: new wine, new skins. Nobody fasts at a wedding feast. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Most churches keep seasons of fasting, especially Lent before Easter, and many Christians connect them with Jesus's words that his followers would fast once the bridegroom was taken away.

chat.says: What did Jesus mean about not putting new wine into old wineskins?
options: New wine is still fermenting and needs a skin that can stretch; what he brings needs room.
That old traditions are worthless and should all be thrown away for good.
That fasting was over for good, and no follower should ever fast again.
chat.meaning: New wine is still fermenting; an old stiff skin would burst. What Jesus brings needs room to move, a vessel that can stretch.

wineskin.meaning: a bag of goat skin for holding wine

Lent.meaning: the season of fasting before Easter

Pharisees.meaning: Jews who cared deeply about holiness

John the Baptist.meaning: the desert prophet whose followers fasted

notes: Mark 2:22 KJV begins 'And no man putteth'; the quotation drops the opening 'And'. Confirm acceptable.
Wineskins: goat skins; fermenting wine stretches a new skin and bursts an old one. Standard explanation; confirm.
The bridegroom 'taken away' as a hint of the death, and church fasts (Lent) connected with 2:20: common reading; confirm phrasing 'most churches still keep fasts'.
The Luke 5:39 line is paraphrased and used to avoid an 'old = bad' reading; confirm it avoids anti-Jewish supersessionist framing.
